title: Piloting agents in GitHub Copilot - Christopher Harrison, Microsoft
talk_summary: A live, partly-derailed GitHub Copilot lab that spends most of its time on context engineering: instruction files, project structure, issue specificity, and the security sandbox of the Copilot coding agent. The transferable mechanisms are repo-level instruction files, path-scoped instruction files, a pre-baked agent environment setup step, and a locked-down ephemeral sandbox with read-only repo access.

takeaways.technique: Repo-level instruction file (copilot-instructions.md) as always-on context
takeaways.what_they_do: A single markdown file in the repo gives high-level overview, coding standards, language guidance, available scripts, and repo structure; it is automatically included in every chat and coding-agent request.

takeaways.technique: Path-scoped instruction files with 'apply to' globs
takeaways.what_they_do: Task-specific markdown files declare an 'apply to' path pattern (e.g. *.tsx, test_*) so they auto-attach only when the agent touches matching files; others are attached manually per task.
takeaways.evidence_quote: up at the very top you'll notice the apply to and then I can put in a path ... any time that you're working with a file that matches that pattern, it will then automatically apply that instructions file

takeaways.what_they_do: A dedicated setup workflow installs all libraries/frameworks/scripts the agent needs before it starts, so the agent's environment is deterministic and it does not need network access to install things.

takeaways.technique: Ephemeral sandbox with read-only repo and branch-scoped write access
takeaways.what_they_do: Agent runs in a throwaway GitHub Actions space, has read-only access to the repo except one branch named for the issue, and a locked firewall with no external calls unless explicitly opened.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Copilot only has read access to your repository save for the branch that it's going to create ... it does not have access to any external services unless you open up the firewall

takeaways.technique: Agent-run tests are advisory; CI re-runs on the PR behind a human/approval gate
takeaways.what_they_do: The agent runs tests locally during its session, but PR workflows do not auto-run for agent-authored PRs until someone reviews and clicks approve; the same lint/test/security gates apply as for humans.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it has not run those tests. And it's only going to run those tests if I click that button right there ... Just because I introduce AI does not mean that any of the fundamentals of DevOps change

takeaways.technique: Explicit, non-ambiguous issue specs ('don't be passive aggressive')
takeaways.what_they_do: Issue text states the desired outcome and the intended approach explicitly, because the agent works asynchronously and cannot be asked follow-ups mid-run.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the more that you leave for the other party to figure out ... the more chance that you're going to come back to something that you really didn't exactly want
